rejection_reason: Contrast, not prefigurement: earlier raisings (Zarephath's son, Lazarus) are distinguished from Christ's resurrection ('first to rise not to die again'), emphasizing difference rather than the earlier ones prefiguring his.

extraction.type_name: Adam's transgression in Paradise / The tree of knowledge of good and evil
extraction.type_description: Adam's eating of the forbidden fruit in Genesis 3, which brought knowledge of good and evil and resulted in death and guilt through transgression of God's commandment
extraction.antitype_name: Paul's (and humanity's) experience under the written law
extraction.antitype_description: The condition of those who receive the written law and through knowledge of its precepts become aware of sin, guilt, and spiritual death when they transgress
extraction.reasoning: The commentary explicitly compares Adam's experience with the forbidden fruit to Paul's experience with the law: both involve a commandment given by God, both result in death through transgression, and both show how a good thing (the tree/the law) becomes the occasion for death through human sin. The parallel suggests Adam's fall under the original commandment prefigures humanity's condemnation under the written law at Sinai.

rejection_reason: Illustrative analogy with a condition for antitype: St. Chrysostom compares Adam's transgression to life under the written law; the 'antitype' is the human condition of guilt under law, not an NT person/event.

extraction.type_name: Old Testament Promises regarding Christ
extraction.type_description: The various promises made by God throughout the Old Testament concerning the coming of Christ and His redemptive work
extraction.antitype_name: Jesus Christ and His Fulfillment of All Promises
extraction.antitype_description: Christ as the ultimate fulfillment and realization of all Old Testament promises; the Amen in whom all divine promises find their yes and completion
extraction.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'All the promises made by God, with regard to Christ, are fulfilled in him.' This directly identifies OT promises as types that find their fulfillment (antitype) in the person and work of Jesus Christ. The reference to 'Amen' emphasizes Christ as the confirmed reality of what was promised in the OT.

rejection_reason: General promise-fulfillment, no specific type: 'All the promises made by God, with regard to Christ, are fulfilled in him' — the Amen — without a defined OT type→antitype pair.

extraction.type_name: The Fading Light on Moses' Face
extraction.type_description: The transient glory/light that surrounded Moses' face, which represented the temporary and weakening nature of the Mosaic law
extraction.antitype_name: The Permanent Glory of Christ / The New Covenant
extraction.antitype_description: The enduring and surpassing glory of the New Covenant in Christ, which does not fade but remains and increases in splendor
extraction.reasoning: The commentary presents the fading light as an allegorical representation of the law's temporary nature. While less explicit as a formal type, this symbolic connection between the transient Mosaic glory and the permanent glory of the New Covenant reflects typological thinking about covenant fulfillment.

rejection_reason: Overlapping: the fading light on Moses's face is part of the same veil/old-covenant typology captured in extraction 0.

extraction.type_name: Mount Sinai
extraction.type_description: The mountain in Arabia where the law was delivered to Moses; represents the former covenant and the servitude of the law
extraction.antitype_name: The Heavenly Jerusalem
extraction.antitype_description: The celestial Jerusalem in heaven, mother of Christians who are no longer servants to the former law but free sons of God through Christ's grace
extraction.reasoning: The commentary describes a mystical affinity between Sinai and earthly Jerusalem (representing the old covenant) versus the heavenly Jerusalem (representing the new covenant and ultimate fulfillment). While not strictly typological in the classical sense, it presents a prefigurative relationship between the earthly law-covenant and the eschatological heavenly reality.

rejection_reason: Contrast, not type→antitype: Sinai/earthly Jerusalem and the heavenly Jerusalem are set in opposition in the allegory (bondage vs freedom), not the one prefiguring the other.

extraction.type_name: Old Testament Types, Figures, and Prophecies concerning the Messiah
extraction.type_description: The collective system of OT types, figures, and prophecies that prefigured the coming Messiah and his redemptive work
extraction.antitype_name: Jesus Christ and His Fulfillment
extraction.antitype_description: Christ's incarnation, life, death, and resurrection, which fulfills all the types, figures, and prophecies of the Old Testament
extraction.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that Christ accomplishes 'all things in heaven and on earth...on earth, by fulfilling all the types, figures, and prophecies concerning the Messias.' This is a direct statement of typological fulfillment where OT types find their antitype in Christ.

rejection_reason: Sweeping general statement: Christ fulfilling 'all the types, figures, and prophecies concerning the Messias' (recapitulation) — no specific OT type→antitype pair.

extraction.type_name: Old Testament prefigurations of a unified people of God
extraction.type_description: The OT types and patterns that pointed to a people composed of both Jews and Gentiles united in worship
extraction.antitype_name: The Church (composed of Jews and Gentiles)
extraction.antitype_description: The New Testament Church formed as 'one great body of true adorers; composed, without distinction, of Jew and Gentile,' uniting the Church triumphant and Church militant under Christ
extraction.reasoning: While the commentary does not explicitly use the word 'type' for this relationship, it describes how God's design to unite Jews and Gentiles was progressively revealed and fulfilled in the formation of the Church. This represents a typological pattern where OT separation and anticipation gives way to NT fulfillment in unified ecclesial reality.

rejection_reason: General and implicit: the formation of one body of Jew and Gentile — no specific OT type is named, only the broad pattern.

extraction.type_name: The ancient figures and prophecies of the former law
extraction.type_description: The Old Testament types, figures, and prophetic prefigurations that were established under the Mosaic law
extraction.antitype_name: Christ and all things established/recapitulated in Christ
extraction.antitype_description: Jesus Christ as the fulfillment in whom all Old Testament types, figures, and prophecies are simultaneously fulfilled and gathered together
extraction.reasoning: St. Jerome's explicit statement that Christ 'fulfills at once in Christ all the ancient figures and prophecies of the former law' directly describes a typological relationship where OT types find their ultimate fulfillment in the person of Christ. The term 'recapitulate' (anakephalaiosasthai) means to gather up or sum up, indicating that Christ is the apex toward which all OT types pointed.

rejection_reason: General recapitulation statement: Christ 'fulfils at once... all the ancient figures and prophecies of the former law' — the holistic principle, not a discrete type-antitype pair.

extraction.type_name: Water effusion in baptismal ritual
extraction.type_description: The physical application of water to the body in the baptismal ceremony, as practiced in Old Testament purification rituals and Jewish ablutions
extraction.antitype_name: The effusion of the Holy Spirit in the soul
extraction.antitype_description: The spiritual renewal and sanctification of the soul through the indwelling and action of the Holy Spirit in the New Testament sacrament of Baptism, making one a child of God
extraction.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'The effusion of the water upon the body in baptism, is a figure of the salutary effusion of the holy Spirit in the soul.' This directly connects the OT practice of water purification (the type) to its NT fulfillment in Christian baptism as a means of spiritual renewal through the Holy Spirit (the antitype). The language of 'figure' confirms a typological relationship.

rejection_reason: Sacramental sign→grace within the rite, not OT typology: 'the effusion of the water upon the body in baptism is a figure of the... effusion of the holy Spirit' — the visible sign signifying invisible grace within baptism, not an OT type prefiguring an NT antitype.

extraction.type_name: Abraham's Covenant Promise
extraction.type_description: God's promise to Abraham to bless all nations through his seed, sealed with an oath
extraction.antitype_name: Christ and the Gospel
extraction.antitype_description: The fulfillment of Abraham's covenant through the coming of Christ, who brings blessing to all nations and establishes the new covenant
extraction.reasoning: The commentary states: 'For God promising to Abraham, to bless all nations in his seed; that is by the coming of Christ.' This identifies the Abrahamic promise as a type fulfilled in Christ's person and redemptive work.

rejection_reason: Promise-fulfillment, no specific type: God's oath to Abraham to bless all nations 'in his seed, that is by the coming of Christ' — covenantal fulfillment, not a defined OT person/event prefiguring an antitype.

extraction.type_name: Melchizedek
extraction.type_description: The king of Salem and priest of the Most High God who blessed Abraham and received tithes from him. Described as without genealogy, without beginning of days or end of life (in the scriptural record). He offered sacrifice of bread and wine.
extraction.antitype_name: Jesus Christ
extraction.antitype_description: Christ who is a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek (Psalm 109:4), fulfilling the priesthood prefigured by Melchizedek and surpassing the Levitical order.
extraction.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that Melchizedek 'is a figure of Christ' and the apostle (in Hebrews) demonstrates that Melchizedek prefigures Christ's eternal priesthood. The typological connection is reinforced by the lack of genealogical record (prefiguring Christ's eternal nature) and the offering of bread and wine (prefiguring the Eucharist/sacrifice of the Mass).

rejection_reason: Duplicate within the Hebrews 7 block: Melchizedek→Christ's priesthood already captured at Heb 7:1 (item 437).

extraction.type_name: Melchisedech's Priesthood
extraction.type_description: The ancient priesthood of Melchisedech, characterized by being eternal (without beginning or end of days according to Scripture), blessing Abraham, and receiving tithes from him, thus demonstrating superiority over the Levitical priesthood
extraction.antitype_name: Christ's Eternal Priesthood
extraction.antitype_description: Christ as the eternal High Priest according to the order of Melchisedech, who rose from death and continues as priest forever without successor, offering one perfect sacrifice for all humanity's sins, conferring inward graces and eternal salvation
extraction.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that Melchisedech's priesthood 'was a figure of the eternal priesthood of Christ.' The type prefigures the antitype through: (1) eternal/perpetual nature; (2) superiority to the Levitical priesthood; (3) offering of blessing; (4) receipt of honor through tithes. The antitype fulfills all these characteristics in Christ's actual priesthood.

rejection_reason: Duplicate: Melchizedek's priesthood→Christ's eternal priesthood already captured at Heb 7:1.

extraction.type_name: Moses and the Law
extraction.type_description: Moses as the mediator who began the dispensation through the law
extraction.antitype_name: Jesus Christ as the New High Priest
extraction.antitype_description: Jesus Christ who completes and perfects what Moses began, serving as the ultimate high priest of the new covenant
extraction.reasoning: The commentary contrasts Moses beginning by the law with Jesus finishing by the gospel, positioning Jesus as the fulfillment of the Mosaic priesthood. While implicit rather than explicit, this reflects a typological relationship where the Mosaic mediatorial role prefigures Christ's role.

rejection_reason: Overlaps extraction 0: Moses beginning by the law / Christ finishing by the gospel is the same law→gospel transition.

extraction.type_name: The Levitical High Priest's Intercession
extraction.type_description: The Old Testament high priest who made intercession for the people of Israel, particularly through the sacrificial system and priestly ministry on their behalf
extraction.antitype_name: Christ as High Priest Making Intercession
extraction.antitype_description: Jesus Christ, as the ultimate High Priest, continually makes intercession for believers by presenting His passion (sacrifice) to God the Father
extraction.reasoning: Hebrews 7 explicitly develops the typology of the Levitical priesthood prefiguring Christ's eternal priesthood. The commentary directly connects the OT priestly function of intercession to Christ's heavenly intercession, which is the primary argument of Hebrews 7. Christ fulfills and supersedes the type of the high priest's mediatorial role.

rejection_reason: Duplicate (and thin commentary): the Levitical high priest's intercession→Christ's intercession restates the ot-priesthood→Christ relationship already captured at Heb 7:4.

extraction.type_name: Jewish Sanctuary/Temple
extraction.type_description: The tabernacle of Moses and temple of Solomon, constructed by human hands as places of worship with a holy of holies
extraction.antitype_name: Heaven/The True Holy of Holies
extraction.antitype_description: The heavenly sanctuary where Christ has entered as the true high priest, prepared by God rather than human hands
extraction.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'the Jewish sanctuary was only a type or figure' of heaven, and contrasts the human-made earthly sanctuary with the divine work of God in heaven. This prefigurement relates to the eschaton (final, heavenly reality).

rejection_reason: Duplicate: Holy of Holies→heaven already captured at Heb 6:13 (item 436).

extraction.type_name: Jewish High Priesthood and Priestly Ministry
extraction.type_description: The OT system of priests ministering in the sanctuary under the former law
extraction.antitype_name: Jesus Christ as Sovereign High Priest
extraction.antitype_description: Christ as the true and ultimate priest who exercises his priesthood both in heaven and upon earth over both the Church triumphant and militant
extraction.reasoning: The commentary describes Christ entering 'the true holy of holies' and being 'the sovereign priest of both' the heavenly and earthly churches, presenting him as the fulfillment of the OT priestly office.

rejection_reason: Duplicate: Jewish high priesthood→Christ already captured (ot-priesthood→christ-high-priest, Heb 7:4).

extraction.type_name: The Levitical sacrificial system / Old Testament priesthood offerings
extraction.type_description: The Old Testament high priests who were ordained to offer gifts and sacrifices to God on behalf of the people
extraction.antitype_name: Christ as the eternal High Priest offering his merits and satisfactions
extraction.antitype_description: Christ, as a priest forever in heaven, offers to God the Father the infinite merits and satisfactions of his death and passion, which he continues to offer through the ministry of His priests on earth
extraction.reasoning: The commentary explicitly establishes that the Old Testament pattern of high priests offering sacrifices prefigures Christ's priesthood and his eternal offering. The verse states 'For every high priest...so Christ, a priest for ever, has now in heaven something to offer.' This is a direct type-antitype correspondence where the OT priestly sacrifice system anticipates and is fulfilled in Christ's eternal priestly ministry.

rejection_reason: Duplicate: Levitical offerings→Christ's offering restates ot-priesthood→christ-high-priest (Heb 7:4).

extraction.type_name: The Priesthood of the Law
extraction.type_description: The Old Testament priesthood and its liturgical functions under the Mosaic covenant
extraction.antitype_name: Christ's Priesthood in His Church
extraction.antitype_description: Christ's priestly ministry and intercession exercised in the Church militant (on earth) and triumphant (in heaven)
extraction.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states the OT priesthood and its functions were 'a kind of an example, and shadow' of what Christ does as priest in His Church. This is classic typological language (shadow/fulfillment pattern), connecting OT type to NT antitype.

rejection_reason: Duplicate: priesthood of the law→Christ's priesthood already captured (Heb 7:4).

extraction.type_name: The Tabernacle
extraction.type_description: The Old Testament tabernacle and its structure as the dwelling place of God and center of worship
extraction.antitype_name: The Church Militant and Triumphant
extraction.antitype_description: The Church as God's dwelling place and the locus of Christ's priestly ministry both on earth and in heaven
extraction.reasoning: The commentary identifies the tabernacle as 'a pattern' (Greek: typos) of the Church. The tabernacle prefigures the Church as the community where Christ exercises His priestly functions and where God dwells, both in its earthly and heavenly dimensions.

rejection_reason: Duplicate: tabernacle→Church already captured at Heb 8:2 (item 442).

extraction.type_name: The Holy of Holies
extraction.type_description: The innermost sanctuary of the Old Testament tabernacle, restricted from entry except by the high priest once yearly, symbolizing God's dwelling place and inaccessible holiness
extraction.antitype_name: Heaven
extraction.antitype_description: The eternal dwelling place of God in the New Testament, made accessible to all believers through Christ's redemptive work
extraction.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'The holy of holies was a figure of heaven' and describes how the OT prohibition against entering prefigured the closed access to heaven under the old covenant, which was opened by Christ's ascension

rejection_reason: Duplicate: Holy of Holies→heaven already captured at Heb 6:13 (item 436).

extraction.type_name: Old Law (sacrifices and sacraments of the old law)
extraction.type_description: The sacrificial system, rituals, and sacraments of the Old Testament law, which provided only a shadow or imperfect representation of spiritual realities
extraction.antitype_name: New Law (blessings of interior graces, remission of sins, true sanctification in Christ)
extraction.antitype_description: The fulfillment in Christ of the spiritual realities prefigured by OT sacrifices—actual remission of sins, interior grace, and true sanctification achieved through faith in Christ
extraction.reasoning: The commentary explicitly uses the shadow/substance metaphor (skian...ouk auten ten eikona) to describe how OT sacrificial law prefigures the reality of NT redemption and sanctification. The commentary states the old sacrifices were 'but a shadow' while 'now in the new law we have an express image of them, that is we have these blessings themselves.' This is a direct type-antitype relationship showing OT institutions pointing forward to their NT fulfillment.

rejection_reason: Duplicate: old-law sacrifices (shadow)→new-covenant graces restates ot-sacrifices→new-covenant already captured at Heb 9:16 (item 446).

extraction.type_name: The Levitical Sacrificial System (particularly the sin offering)
extraction.type_description: The Old Testament system of animal sacrifices, especially those offered for expiation and sanctification on the Day of Atonement
extraction.antitype_name: The Eucharistic Sacrifice
extraction.antitype_description: The Eucharist as the continuation of Christ's sacrifice on the cross in a different manner, perpetuating the sacrificial offering in sacramental form
extraction.reasoning: The commentary interprets this passage as referring to the sacrifice of the Eucharist, which continues Christ's sacrifice 'though in a different manner.' This represents the OT sacrificial system being fulfilled and transformed into the sacramental form of the Eucharist.

rejection_reason: Duplicate: Levitical sacrifices→Eucharist already captured at Heb 8:3 (item 443).

extraction.type_name: Anointing with oil in miraculous healings (Mark 6:13)
extraction.type_description: The anointing of sick persons with oil performed by the apostles and disciples during their miraculous healings in the apostolic era
extraction.antitype_name: Extreme Unction (Sacrament of Anointing of the Sick)
extraction.antitype_description: The sacrament of extreme unction instituted by Christ and described by St. James, using oil to strengthen the souls of the sick against dangers and temptations at the approach of death
extraction.reasoning: The commentary states: 'the anointing in St. Mark, used in corporal diseases, may be looked upon as a figure of the sacrament of extreme unction in St. James.' While this is explicitly stated as a typological relationship, it represents a transition from miraculous/physical healing to spiritual/sacramental purpose rather than a classical OT-to-NT type.

rejection_reason: Intra-NT, not OT typology: the apostolic anointing of the sick (Mark 6:13) 'looked upon as a figure of the sacrament of extreme unction' (James 5) — both are NT texts.

extraction.type_name: Isaiah's prophetic descriptions of God as 'First and Last'
extraction.type_description: The Old Testament prophet Isaiah applies the titles 'first and last' to God, expressing His eternal nature and divine attributes (see Isaiah 41:4, 44:6, 48:12)
extraction.antitype_name: Christ as 'First and Last' in Revelation 1:17
extraction.antitype_description: Jesus Christ, the Son of man appearing to John in the Revelation, claims the same titles ('I am the first and the last'), affirming His divinity and eternal nature as the true God
extraction.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that the expression 'first and last' is 'another expression agreeing only to him who is the true God, as it is divers times applied by the prophet Isaias.' This demonstrates a direct typological transfer where Isaiah's Old Testament descriptions of God's eternal nature find their fulfillment in Christ's self-identification in the New Testament.

rejection_reason: Divine-title application, not typology: 'First and Last' (Isaiah's title of God) applied to Christ proves his divinity — a title transfer affirming Christ is God, not an OT type prefiguring an NT antitype.

extraction.type_name: The Ancient of Days' Judgment Scene in Daniel
extraction.type_description: In Daniel 7:9-10, thrones are placed and the Ancient of Days sits in judgment, with the judgment sitting and books being opened before pronouncing sentence against Antiochus Epiphanes
extraction.antitype_name: The Twenty-Four Elders' Judgment Scene in Revelation
extraction.antitype_description: The four and twenty elders sitting around God's throne in Revelation 4:4, representing the judgment about to be passed upon the enemies of the Church
extraction.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'Thus in Daniel...thrones were placed, and the ancient of days sat' as a direct parallel to the Revelation scene, indicating the OT prophecy prefigures the NT fulfillment of divine judgment in the eschatological vision

rejection_reason: Parallel apocalyptic imagery: Daniel's throne/judgment scene (Dan 7) is cross-referenced as 'like' the Revelation scene — the same eschatological judgment depicted twice, not a type-antitype prefigurement.

extraction.type_name: The Patriarchs and Apostles as Judges
extraction.type_description: The ancient patriarchs (OT figures) who are designated as judges alongside God
extraction.antitype_name: The Twenty-Four Elders (12 Patriarchs + 12 Apostles)
extraction.antitype_description: The elders in Revelation 4:4 representing both Old and New Testament saints who judge with the Lord and condemn the injustice of persecutors
extraction.reasoning: The commentary suggests the number 24 designates 'the ancient patriarchs and the twelve apostles, who judge with the Lord,' indicating the OT patriarchs' role as judges prefigures their ultimate eschatological role in the heavenly judgment depicted in Revelation

rejection_reason: Identification, not typology: the 24 elders are explained as the patriarchs and apostles — an interpretation of who they are, not a defined OT type→NT antitype.

extraction.type_name: The Four Major Prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel)
extraction.type_description: Four Old Testament prophets whose prophetic ministries, characterized by divine inspiration and supernatural sight into past, present, and future, are symbolically represented by four living creatures with multiple eyes and wings
extraction.antitype_name: The Heavenly Worship and Prophetic Fulfillment in Revelation
extraction.antitype_description: In the New Testament vision of Revelation 4, these four prophets are exalted in heaven as representatives of all Old Testament prophecy, standing before God's throne and participating in eternal worship, signifying the fulfillment and vindication of Old Testament prophetic witness
extraction.reasoning: The commentary identifies a progression from OT prophetic ministry to their exaltation in the NT eschatological vision. The four prophets' characteristics (omniscient sight, divine inspiration) prefigure their role in the heavenly revelation to John. However, this is somewhat attenuated typology—it represents symbolic continuity and fulfillment rather than a strict prefigurement of a single antitype, making it less explicit than classical typology.

rejection_reason: Symbolic identification: the four living creatures are interpreted as the four major prophets — an allegorical reading of the vision, not a prefigurement (and disputed: '30 different expositions').

extraction.type_name: The Seraphim of Isaiah's Vision (Isaiah 6:2)
extraction.type_description: OT celestial beings described with six wings attending God's throne in Isaiah's prophetic vision
extraction.antitype_name: The Four Living Creatures in Revelation 4
extraction.antitype_description: NT heavenly beings with six wings standing before God's throne in John's apocalyptic vision, representing the continuity and fulfillment of prophetic witness to God's majesty
extraction.reasoning: The commentary explicitly notes the four living creatures have 'six wings, in the same manner as the seraphim appeared to the prophet Isaias.' This connects an OT theophanic vision to its NT counterpart in Revelation, suggesting the seraphim's form prefigures the form of heavenly worship revealed to John.

rejection_reason: Parallel celestial imagery: the creatures have six wings 'as the seraphim appeared to Isaias' — a cross-reference of similar imagery, not type-antitype.

extraction.type_name: The four living creatures of Ezekiel's vision
extraction.type_description: The six-winged creatures full of eyes described in Ezekiel 1:4 and Isaiah 6:2, representing celestial beings that serve as witnesses to God's glory and execute His commands with swiftness
extraction.antitype_name: The four living creatures around God's throne in Revelation 4
extraction.antitype_description: The eschatological vision of the four living creatures in heaven who continuously praise God, signifying eternal worship and the uninterrupted adoration that characterizes the heavenly reality
extraction.reasoning: The commentary explicitly directs readers to 'See the like visions, Ezechiel 1:4; Isaias 6:2,' establishing a direct connection between the OT prophetic visions and the NT apocalyptic vision. The OT visions prefigure the heavenly worship scene in Revelation, which represents the ultimate fulfillment of eternal worship in the eschaton.

rejection_reason: Parallel apocalyptic imagery: 'See the like visions, Ezech 1:4; Isa 6:2' cross-references the same celestial beings/heavenly worship across OT and NT visions — not a defined prefigurement.

extraction.type_name: Living waters/fountains of life (OT imagery)
extraction.type_description: Old Testament references to life-giving waters as divine blessing and sustenance, representing God's provision and the source of eternal life
extraction.antitype_name: Fountains of living waters in heaven
extraction.antitype_description: In Revelation 7:17, the redeemed are led to fountains of living waters as the fulfillment of eternal refreshment, life, and happiness in the eschaton
extraction.reasoning: The commentary notes Christ 'shall lead them unto fountains of living waters' as a representation of heavenly happiness. While this draws on OT water imagery (Psalm 23:2, Isaiah 55:1, Jeremiah 2:13), the connection is somewhat implicit rather than explicitly framed as typology in the commentary itself, making it a supporting rather than primary typological relationship.

rejection_reason: Implicit imagery, not asserted as a figura: 'fountains of living waters' draws on OT water imagery but the commentary makes no explicit type-antitype claim (extraction concedes it is 'somewhat implicit').

extraction.type_name: The Four Great Empires (Daniel 7 - Chaldean, Persian, Grecian, Roman)
extraction.type_description: In Daniel 7, four beasts represent four great empires: the leopard (Chaldean), bear (Persian), lion (Grecian/Alexander), and composite beast (Roman). These symbolize successive earthly kingdoms.
extraction.antitype_name: The Beast of Revelation 13 and its composite appearance
extraction.antitype_description: The second beast in Revelation 13 is described with resemblances of a leopard, bear, and lion, alluding to Daniel's four empires. This represents the final idolatrous Roman empire and its persecuting powers under emperors like Diocletian and Julian.
extraction.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states: 'The resemblances of a leopard, bear, and lion, are introduced with an allusion to what is written by the prophet Daniel, (Daniel vii.) meaning the four great empires.' This is a direct typological connection where Daniel's prophetic beasts prefigure the beasts of Revelation describing end-times persecution.

rejection_reason: Duplicate: Daniel's four empires→the beast of Revelation already captured at Rev 13:2 (item 463).

extraction.type_name: Satan's deceptions in the Book of Job (Job 1 - divine permission for supernatural acts)
extraction.type_description: In Job 1, the devil was permitted by God to perform supernatural acts (making fire come from heaven) to test Job's faith, demonstrating Satan's limited power under divine constraint.
extraction.antitype_name: False prophets performing great wonders in the end times (Matthew 24:24, Revelation 13:12)
extraction.antitype_description: Christ foretold that false prophets would perform great wonders and miracles in the latter days. The second beast causes fire to come from heaven (similar to Job's experience), deceiving many into worshiping the antichrist.
extraction.reasoning: The commentary connects Job's experience of demonic deception ('making even fire by lightning come from heaven, as the devil was permitted to do in the time of Job') to the end-times deceptions described in Matthew 24:24 and Revelation 13:12. While not a classical typology, it establishes a pattern of Satanic deception permitted by God that recurs in eschatological contexts.

rejection_reason: Pattern of Satanic activity, not typology: 'as the devil was permitted to do in the time of Job' compares end-times false wonders to Job's testing — a recurring pattern, not a defined type-antitype (extraction concedes 'not a classical typology').

extraction.type_name: The binding of Satan (implied OT precedent)
extraction.type_description: OT prophecies regarding God's restraint of evil and Satan's limitations, grounded in divine sovereignty over creation
extraction.antitype_name: Christ's binding of Satan through His incarnation and passion
extraction.antitype_description: Christ's first coming and crucifixion, which greatly diminished Satan's power over the nations, restricting his ability to tempt and persecute, lasting throughout the entire Christian age until his final loosing before the end times
extraction.reasoning: The commentary states that 'the power of Satan has been very much abridged by the passion of Christ' and that Satan is 'bound' (his power 'restrained') from Christ's first coming onward. While not explicitly citing an OT type, this represents the antitype of OT restraint of evil, with Christ's work being the fulfillment of God's sovereign limitation of demonic power.

rejection_reason: No explicit OT type: the binding of Satan by Christ's passion is the antitype, but the 'type' is only a vague 'OT precedent of God restraining evil' — no defined OT person/event/institution (extraction concedes 'implied... no explicit OT type').
